title: Higher Yields Are Here to Stay - Systematic Investor - Ep.350

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Higher Yields Are Here to Stay - Systematic Investor - Ep.350.docx

speakers: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged, CTA background)
Alan Dunne (co-host, allocator/researcher, Substack Beyond the Cycle)
summary: Systematic Investor ep. 350 (30 May 2025): Alan lays out why all roads lead to higher bond yields (US deficits and debt, R-minus-G, fiscal dominance, weaker bond diversification), then Niels and Alan review a weak May for trend followers, the SG Prime allocator survey, and asset allocation (scenario analysis, forward-looking return estimates, US re-rating). Conclusion: robust portfolios need non-predictive diversifiers such as trend following, and trend allocations should not be timed on macro views.

coverage.note: intro; patchy tariff-distorted economic data and effect on macro strategies
port of LA, private equity exits to retail, low DPI, private credit diversification
Japan 40-year auction, yen carry puzzle, BOJ losses, Bitcoin market cap
intro to All Roads Lead to Higher Yields; 1993 Carville comparison of fiscal position
1993-2010 fiscal history: Clinton tax hike, Greenspan, surplus, austerity
2017 tax cut, MMT, Covid and Biden spending, end of neoliberal era, R minus G
debt arithmetic, vicious cycle, recession vs inflation scenarios, Fed chair, fiscal dominance
narrative of ignoring debt, growth cannot solve it, credible policy needed
Stargate energy use, politicians vs central banks, real yields and term premium
tariffs and full employment, Section 899, May trend update
May trend dynamics, model speed, index data
discretionary macro vs rules-based, pod shops, asset allocation framework anchoring
scenario-based allocation, investment returns yearbook, forward vs past returns
US re-rating, required vs expected returns, forward-looking estimates
forward-looking measures and drawdowns; trend as plan for unforeseen risks
robust portfolios, diversification, do not link trend to macro view, drawdown not unusual
nothing actionable: do not time it (repeats C17), sign-off

completeness_estimate: 0.94 - first reader caught almost all ideas (73 claims); missed the Eichengreen debt point, bill-heavy issuance, the inflation-led yield scenario, and Alan's disagreement on discretionary macro; two speaker errors in C17.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: just the the variability and the, you know, patchiness of the economic data because of all of the disruptions that we've seen
claims.claim: Tariff announcements, pauses and court rulings make economic data unusually patchy, so reading the economy from hard data will be difficult for months.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: obviously what you've seen is a lot of um stockpiling or a lot of activity ahead of the tariffs. Then you had a pause when the tariffs came in.
claims.claim: Front-loading before tariffs followed by a pause distorts durable goods orders (down 7% after +6-7% the previous month), so single prints mislead.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: You know the soft data the sentiment data already showing a lot of pessimism and big impacts uh h in terms of consumer and business uh sentiment.
claims.claim: Soft sentiment data show strong pessimism while hard data are noisy, creating a hard-vs-soft gap and an unclear turning point for the economy.
claims.indicator: consumer and business sentiment vs hard data

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: arguably it has obvious implications for for any strategies that are based on, you know, a read of that the the kind of the high frequency macro data.
claims.claim: Noisy macro data harm strategies built on high-frequency macro data, so such macro strategies face a tricky period.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: even if you do a pause of 90 days, it's not really long enough for companies to uh essentially uh get the the things produced in China.
claims.claim: Port of Los Angeles bookings rose less than expected during the 90-day tariff pause since production and shipping lead times exceed the pause.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: worrying signs that a lot of these private equity uh products were now being lined up to be sold to private investors, to retail investors, packaged.
claims.claim: Thoma Bravo's co-founder sees private equity exits being packaged for retail investors as a sign of no institutional demand.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the low kind of level of cash coming back from private equity transactions
claims.claim: Low distributions (DPI) from private equity constrain new flows into the asset class, which is why the last buyer may be retail or high net worth investors.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: people shouldn't think that that there's a lot of diversification um in in private credit. I mean, it's all kind of the same type of sectors and industries
claims.claim: Private credit offers less diversification than assumed because it holds the same sectors, industries and weaker credit ratings.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: And now you're really seeing how yields, especially in the long end, are really really surging in in in Japan.
claims.claim: Surging long-end Japanese yields (weak 40-year auction) matter globally because Japanese investors become less incentivized to buy foreign debt.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the whole um incentive to go out and buy foreign debt, which we'll talk about later on, um you know, dwindles when you see something like this.
claims.claim: Higher domestic Japanese yields reduce Japanese demand for foreign bonds.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the obvious then next point is oh this is going to see a huge unwinding of the carry trade but you know dollar yen has hardly moved
claims.claim: The JGB yield spike did not trigger yen carry unwinding; dollar-yen stayed in range, possibly because insurers shifted from 40-year to 10-year bonds.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the BOJ bought a lot of the bonds ahead of the move. So I mean they effectively subsidized the private sector
claims.claim: The BOJ's earlier bond purchases shifted losses from the private sector to the central bank, so the yield rise did not cause private-sector stress.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: BTC's market cap stands at 2.12 trillion higher than the market cap of Alphabet/Google.
claims.claim: Bitcoin hit new all-time highs in late May 2025 with a market cap above Alphabet's (unverified).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: deficit, it was about bit more than 4% of GDP and the debt to GDP ratio was about 45% of G GDP
claims.claim: In 1993 the bond market intimidated politicians at a deficit of about 4% of GDP and debt of 45% of GDP with 10-year yields near 6%, versus roughly 100% debt/GDP today.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the big beautiful bill going through Congress which is going to add another nearly 4 trillion to the deficit over the next 10 years
claims.claim: The 2025 budget bill adds nearly 4 trillion over ten years to US deficits, adding to the debt supply.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: back 32 years ago the bond market could still be an influence uh on on on politicians on policy even at much lower levels of of debt and at lower levels of deficits
claims.claim: Bond market discipline of fiscal policy has weakened: it constrained politicians at far lower debt and deficits in 1993 than today.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the best thing he could do in terms of getting lower rates would be to cut the deficit because that would make it easier for the Fed to pursue an easier policy
claims.claim: In the 1990s deficit reduction (Clinton tax hikes) allowed easier Fed policy and lower yields, which fueled investment; the opposite fiscal stance today does not help.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: by 2019 you know the deficit was back to like 4 and a half% the same as the Clinton era but this time for an economy at full employment
claims.claim: From 2017 the US ran large deficits at full employment, a procyclical turning point, followed by MMT ideas and huge Covid spending.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the idea of fiscal conservatism was was gone
claims.claim: The end of the neoliberal era made fiscal conservatism disappear, so no political or ideological appetite to cut deficits exists even as supply chains and industrial policy add cost.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: higher inflation does kind of reduce um the real value of debt. Um but now as inflation's coming down the real value of debt has moving up again.
claims.claim: The 2021-22 inflation eroded real debt but disinflation reverses this, so the debt burden rises again.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: your debt servicing cost rises above your growth rate that means more and more of your resources are going on um on servicing the debt
claims.claim: When interest rates exceed growth (R greater than G), debt service takes a growing share of resources and debt becomes unsustainable regardless of the debt/GDP level.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if yields spike up to 5% or above then that shifts that relationship that you're or exceeds your growth and would negatively impact the growth outlook
claims.claim: With nominal GDP growth of 4-4.5% and 10-year yields at that level, a spike to 5% or more breaks R-G and hurts growth and fiscal arithmetic.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the higher yields go it makes the debt less sustainable. So you're into a vicious cycle then of higher yields a more pessimistic uh outlook.
claims.claim: Higher yields make debt less sustainable, which raises yields further: a self-reinforcing loop.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if we had a recession, it would probably bring yields back down because the Fed would probably ease
claims.claim: A recession would pull yields down short-term as the Fed eases, as seen in the last 2-3 years where deficit worries fade on weak data.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: then automatic stabilizers kicking. More people claim unemployment assistance. There could be another fiscal stimulus.
claims.claim: A recession would widen the deficit via automatic stabilizers and stimulus, so it delays rather than solves the fiscal problem.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Nixon and Arthur Arthur Burns is a classic example of of having a Fed chair who was sympathetic or or at least under the influence of of the administration
claims.claim: The next Fed chair when Powell's term ends in 2026 is a risk because a chair under administration influence (Nixon/Burns) could ease too much, pushing yields up.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: either financial repression this idea of you know having to force um institutions to to to to buy bonds whether it's the Fed or or the private sector
claims.claim: Most scenarios end in financial repression or fiscal dominance (forced bond buying or easier-than-warranted policy).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: these crisis take longer to evolve than you expect but when they happen then they are much more dramatic and and and fast moving than you thought possible
claims.claim: Dornbusch: fiscal crises develop slowly then move fast, so timing the bond market break is hard but the direction is clear.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I think all roads do lead to higher yields.
claims.claim: The thesis: debt, deficits and policy over 30 years point to higher yields, whether this year or next.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we've now crossed from this might you know the debt might be unsustainable to obviously it is unsustainable but the problem is nobody cares about it
claims.claim: Ben Hunt's narrative view: debt is acknowledged as unsustainable but no one acts, so the market can ignore it until something shifts the narrative.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it was strong growth in the decades after it that helped pull pull down the US debt to GDP level
claims.claim: After WWII strong growth reduced the debt/GDP ratio, but repeating that is unlikely now given labor force limits (immigration, aging) and AI productivity lags.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the internet came in the late '9s it was maybe 10 15 years later before the productivity gains were really seen
claims.claim: Productivity gains from new technology (AI) typically lag adoption by 10-15 years, so growth will not fix the debt soon.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you stop it by coming up with a credible policy to address the deficit
claims.claim: A fast yield spike (5% to 6%) would only stop with a credible deficit policy, which is politically unlikely.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I think we'll have to uh hit the wall before something happens.
claims.claim: Politicians act on deficits only after a crisis forces them to.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they estimate it's going to be using as much energy as 750,000 homes
claims.claim: The Stargate AI data center in Texas will use energy equal to 750,000 homes, an example of AI-driven power demand.
claims.indicator: power demand from AI data centers

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: someone said to me we go through cycles where you have either strong politicians and weak central banks or vice versa
claims.claim: Policy power alternates between politicians and central banks; today politicians dominate, so inflation becomes a political choice.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we've seen um a big jump in real yields already and from negative obviously before the um you know co to you know real yields US now 2%
claims.claim: US real yields rose from negative to about 2% (vs over 3% in 1993), consistent with rising term premia, and may decouple from inflation.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: when you had that negative correlation between bonds and equities um bonds were quite valuable in your portfolio so you might have been willing to tolerate a smaller term premium
claims.claim: With a negative stock-bond correlation investors accepted a low term premium; as the hedge value fades they require a higher yield.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it's an economy already at full employment. So where do where are the workers going to come from
claims.claim: Reindustrializing a full-employment US economy creates bottlenecks, skill shortages and wage pressure that may spill over to broad inflation.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a little publicized provision in Donald Trump's budget bill that allows the government to raise taxes on foreign investments in the US could upend markets and hit American industry
claims.claim: Section 899 could tax foreign holders of US stocks, bonds and dividends, a risk to foreign demand for US assets.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own trend barometer finished yesterday at 30. That's a low reading. That's a weak reading.
claims.claim: A trend barometer at 30 (end of May 2025) is weak and implies industry losses with dispersion.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: long positions have probably been challenged uh during May uh in particular in the short end
claims.claim: May 2025 hurt longer-term CTAs through long fixed income, coffee corrections and a gold pause, while live cattle helped.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: equities for those who did not flip positions during the April uh period
claims.claim: In May equities favored managers that did not flip positions in April, so model speed determined results.
claims.indicator: model speed in the April reversal

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: this lack of strong signals across uh most markets and that generally leads to to uh trend followers uh cutting risk
claims.claim: Weak signal strength makes trend models cut risk, and with equities near highs they add long risk again.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the medium-term trend followers probably the ones who've had the toughest time compared to being short-term or long-term
claims.claim: In 2025 medium-term trend followers had the toughest time versus short and long term.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: most medium-term would have got on say the long euro trade and short dollar versus say the Swiss or the yen and and those have kind of been choppy and up and down in the range
claims.claim: Medium-term FX trend positions (long euro, short dollar) turned choppy in a range for 4-6 weeks, hurting CTAs.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you're a slow if you're ultra slow and managed to to not react much that was obviously the best thing
claims.claim: Ultra-slow trend followers did best through the April-May equity V-reversal.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: The trend index down 2% uh roughly 2.13% down 11.25% for the year.
claims.claim: As of 28 May 2025 the trend index was down 2.13% in May and 11.25% YTD, with the short-term traders index down 2% YTD, versus the S&P 500 up 1% for the year.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: survey 370 institutional investors or allocators managing trillions of dollars
claims.claim: SG Prime spring 2025 survey: global macro is the strategy most likely to see increased allocation, then equity market neutral, then commodities, with performance chasing a possible factor.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: about 30% of of of allocators were saying that they would considering allocating to CTA trend and a little bit less to CTA non-trend
claims.claim: About 30% of allocators plan to consider trend CTAs, down about 2.5 points from fall 2024, after a tough year.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: quant macro, which again, it's not really the flavor of the month given this kind of market environment
claims.claim: Quant macro and ESG interest declined in the survey, partly because macro data are choppy.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: massively biased here but I'm kind of thinking hm kind of a non-predictive rules-based diversified approach might be quite useful.
claims.claim: When allocators flock to discretionary macro, a non-predictive rules-based diversified approach is useful in unpredictable policy regimes.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: February, March seemed to be tough for them, you know, with particularly the more equity focused ones with the unwind of the momentum um kind of trade in in that period.
claims.claim: Pod shops (multi-strategy funds) were hit in Feb-March 2025 by the momentum unwind but recovered in April-May.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: not kind of anchoring to you know returns volatility estimates correlation estimates to a particular period
claims.claim: Asset allocation inputs should not be anchored to a single period such as 1980-2020, when disinflation and falling yields favored financial assets.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I think that points to you know taking a more of a scenariobased approach to portfolio
claims.claim: Scenario-based portfolio construction is better than plugging in historical averages when the regime is shifting.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: making sure that your your optimization or your allocation process isn't overly sensitive to any assumption around volatility or correlation
claims.claim: Allocation processes should be robust to volatility and correlation assumptions because the future can differ from the past.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you could literally map out asset allocation plans for for different macro scenarios as opposed to just having one base case
claims.claim: Build a portfolio for each macro scenario (stagflation, inflation) and weight by probability; this tilts away from financial assets toward real assets, commodities and pure diversifiers.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they would also have said don't expect the US to continue to outperform the way it has but they were wrong on that
claims.claim: The Global Investment Returns Yearbook warned in 2000 of lower returns (correct) and less US outperformance (wrong), so valuation-based forecasts have limits.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: a big part of the component of um of you know the the US exceptionalism has just been a re-ranking you know a valuation change
claims.claim: US outperformance came largely from re-rating: CAPE went from about half of non-US in 1990 to double today, so mean reversion argues for less US bullishness (AQR paper).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: that would mean the US is a safer place to invest and you're required lower return
claims.claim: Dimson: if the US is safer, its required return is lower, so the bullish US narrative implies lower future returns, an inconsistency between required and expected return views.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: that kind of forward-looking estimate has worked better over time
claims.claim: Forward-looking return estimates (dividend yield plus earnings growth, about 5-6% for US equities) correlate positively with realized 10-year returns, whereas trailing past returns correlate negatively.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: in the good times, better returns tend to get accentuated. In the bad times, it's the same on the downside as well.
claims.claim: Realized returns exceed forward-looking estimates when those are high, and fall short when low (2010 predicted 8-10%, got 15%; 2000 predicted 3-4%, got flat).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: future returns based on these kind of more forward-looking measures are pointing to lower than average returns for equities
claims.claim: Forward-looking measures currently point to below-average equity returns, i.e. downside risk.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: equity drawdowns, big equity drawdowns tend to come following periods of great optimism.
claims.claim: Large equity drawdowns follow periods of optimism and rich valuations, like 2000, rather than pessimism.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you have three or four and you choose the wrong one, it could hurt
claims.claim: Choosing among several regime scenarios raises the risk of picking the wrong one, an argument for trend following.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: But then if you're asking them, so what are you doing about the risks that you haven't thought about? There's nothing on the list, right?
claims.claim: Portfolio managers list known risks but have no answer for unforeseen risks; trend following covers risks nobody planned for.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think our role as trend followers is to play the role where we don't have a specific plan or regime that we are planning for.
claims.claim: The trend follower's role is regime-agnostic positioning, not crisis alpha.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I don't think you build them by having two strong opinions about what's going to happen in a world that seems to be changing
claims.claim: Robust portfolios come from diversification across risk factors, not from strong forecasts.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: diversification is not saying equities private equity credit and private credit and saying we're diversified because you know obviously you're picking up a lot of the same kind of risk there
claims.claim: True diversification means balancing across risk factors; equities, private equity and credit share the same tail risk.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you try and link you know trend following allocation to a particular macro view like that it might you might be right for a year
claims.claim: Allocating to trend following based on a macro view works for about a year before something surprises, so do not link it to the macro outlook.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker: the point that linking trend allocation to a macro view (e.g. 'Trump on-off is bad for trend') works for a year and then surprises is Alan's reply, not Niels's.
correction.fix: Alan Dunne: allocating to trend following based on a macro view may be right for a year before something surprises, so trend allocation should not be tied to the macro outlook.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: removed any knowledge that you might have about politics and who's in the White House and who's not in the White House and all of that, then you would say this is not unusual
claims.claim: The current trend following drawdown looks normal in the drawdown profile; blaming Trump is no excuse.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: often it ends up breaking something that we can then latch on to as trend followers
claims.claim: Political changes may be good or bad for trend followers, but often break something that creates trends.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you wait for it to be very obvious it's going to be you know I would say it was probably by 2022 when it was kind of mainstream
claims.claim: Waiting until the environment looks favorable for trend following means missing years (2019-2021 were good, but consensus came in 2022), so do not time it.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker: the 2016-2022 timing example ending 'Don't try and time it' is Alan's; Niels answers 'Yeah. No, absolutely. Alan, this was great'.
correction.fix: Alan Dunne: waiting until the environment looks favourable for trend following means missing years (2019-2021 were good, consensus only in 2022), so do not time trend allocations.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Barry Iikin Green presented a paper at Jackson Hole two years ago to you know all the good and the great in the central banking community about high debt levels and how they're going to be here to stay
claims.claim: Eichengreen's Jackson Hole paper argued that today's high public debt levels will not be worked down and are here to stay, which underpins the view of persistently higher yields.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: now we're into a situation where you know they can't term out the they had to issue bills because this concern about lack of demand for for the long end
claims.claim: After the 2000 surplus the US even stopped issuing long bonds for a while, but now the Treasury cannot term out its debt and leans on bill issuance because of doubts about demand at the long end of the curve.
claims.testable: yes - bill share of issuance vs term premium

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Another scenario is is the economy doesn't weak that weaken that much and and maybe we see higher inflation in the near term and the Fed might have to actually respond to that.
claims.claim: In the alternative scenario where the economy does not weaken much and near-term inflation rises, a Fed forced to respond becomes the trigger that pushes yields up in the near term.
claims.testable: partly - yield reaction to inflation surprises in non-recession periods

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I just think it is an environment it does offer big opportunities obviously that doesn't mean every discretionary macro manager will be on the right side of it and that's what we saw in April
claims.claim: Contrary to Niels's coin-flip view, Alan argues the high-dispersion 2025 environment offers big asymmetric opportunities for discretionary macro, though results vary widely across managers as April showed.
claims.indicator: macro and CTA manager return dispersion
claims.testable: partly - dispersion of macro fund returns in volatile regimes
